(a) Find the solution $u(x,t)$. Hint: a trig identity.

(b) Find the average temperature.

(c) Initially the temperature variation is 1 (maximum minus the minimum). Find the time when the variation is ${1}/{2}$.

section_title: PDEs, separation of variables, and the heat equation
q:
Find a series solution of

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_t = 3 u_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi \text{ and } t > 0, \\ u(0,t) = u(\pi,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ u(x,0) = 5\sin (x) + 2\sin (5x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi . \end{array}$$

section_title: PDEs, separation of variables, and the heat equation
q:
Find a series solution of

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_t = 0.1 u_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi \text{ and } t > 0, \\ u_x(0,t) = u_x(\pi,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ u(x,0) = 1 + 2\cos (x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi . \end{array}$$

section_title: PDEs, separation of variables, and the heat equation
q: Use separation of variables to find a nontrivial solution to $u_{xt} = u_{xx}$.

section_title: PDEs, separation of variables, and the heat equation
q: Use a variation on separation of variables to find a nontrivial solution to $u_{x} + u_{t} = u$. Hint: Try $u(x,t) = X(x)+T(t)$.

section_title: PDEs, separation of variables, and the heat equation
q:
Suppose that the temperature on the wire is fixed at $0$ at the ends, $L=1$, $k=1$, and $u(x,0) = 100\sin(2 \pi x)$.

(a) What is the temperature at $x = {1}/{2}$ at any time?

(b) What is the maximum and the minimum temperature on the wire at $t=0$?

(c) At what time is the maximum temperature on the wire exactly one half of the initial maximum at $t=0$?
Check that $w(x,0) = 0$ and $w_t(x,0) = g(x)$.

Solve

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = 9 y_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(1,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0 , \\ y(x,0) = \sin (3\pi x) + \frac{1}{4} \sin (6 \pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 , \\ y_t(x,0) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 . \end{array}$$

Solve

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = 4 y_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(1,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ y(x,0) = \sin (3\pi x) + \frac{1}{4} \sin (6 \pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 , \\ y_t(x,0) = \sin (9 \pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 . \end{array}$$
Derive the solution for a general plucked string of length $L$ and any constant $a$ (in the equation $y_{tt} = a^2 y_{xx}$), where we raise the string some distance $b$ at the midpoint and let go.

Imagine that a stringed musical instrument fell on the floor. Suppose that the length of the string is 1 and $a=1$. When the musical instrument hit the ground, the string was in rest position and hence $y(x,0) = 0$. However, the string was moving at some velocity at impact ($t=0$), say $y_t(x,0) = -1$. Find the solution $y(x,t)$ for the shape of the string at time $t$.

Suppose that you have a vibrating string and that there is air resistance proportional to the velocity. That is, you have

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = a^2 y_{xx} - k y_t & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(1,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ y(x,0) = f(x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 , \\ y_t(x,0) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 1 . \end{array}$$

Suppose that $0 < k < 2 \pi a$. Derive a series solution to the problem. Any coefficients in the series should be expressed as integrals of $f(x)$.

Suppose you touch the guitar string exactly in the middle to ensure another condition $y({L}/{2},t) = 0$ for all time. Which multiples of the fundamental frequency $\frac{\pi a}{L}$ show up in the solution?

Solve

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = y_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi, t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(\pi,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ y(x,0) = \sin(x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi , \\ y_t(x,0) = \sin(x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi . \end{array}$$

Solve

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = 25 y_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 2 \text{ and } t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(2,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0, \\ y(x,0) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 2 , \\ y_t(x,0) = \sin(\pi x) + 0.1 \sin(2\pi x) & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < 2 . \end{array}$$

Solve

$$\begin{array}{ll} y_{tt} = 2 y_{xx} & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi \text{ and } t > 0, \\ y(0,t) = y(\pi,t) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; t > 0 , \\ y(x,0) = x & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi , \\ y_t(x,0) = 0 & \qquad \text{for } \; 0 < x < \pi . \end{array}$$
What happens when $a=0$? Find a solution to $y_{tt} = 0$, $y(0,t) = y(\pi,t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = \sin(2x)$, $y_t(x,0) = \sin(x)$.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q: Using the d'Alembert solution solve $y_{tt} = 4y_{xx}$, $0 < x < \pi$, $t > 0$, $y(0,t) = y(\pi, t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = \sin x$, and $y_t(x,0) = \sin x$. Hint: Note that $\sin x$ is the odd periodic extension of $y(x,0)$ and $y_t(x,0)$.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q: Using the d'Alembert solution solve $y_{tt} = 2y_{xx}$, $0 < x < 1$, $t > 0$, $y(0,t) = y(1, t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = \sin^5 (\pi x)$, and $y_t(x,0) = \sin^3 (\pi x)$.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q:
Take $y_{tt} = 4y_{xx}$, $0 < x < \pi$, $t > 0$, $y(0,t) = y(\pi, t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = x(\pi-x)$, and $y_t(x,0) = 0$.

(a) Solve using the d'Alembert formula. Hint: You can use the sine series for $y(x,0)$.

(b) Find the solution as a function of $x$ for a fixed $t=0.5$, $t=1$, and $t=2$. Do not use the sine series here.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q: Derive the d'Alembert solution for $y_{tt} = a^2 y_{xx}$, $0 < x < \pi$, $t > 0$, $y(0,t) = y(\pi, t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = f(x)$, and $y_t(x,0) = 0$, using the Fourier series solution of the wave equation, by applying an appropriate trigonometric identity. Hint: Do it first for a single term of the Fourier series solution, in particular do it when $y$ is $\sin(n x )\cos(n a t )$.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q:
The d'Alembert solution still works if there are no boundary conditions and the initial condition is defined on the whole real line. Suppose that $y_{tt} = y_{xx}$ (for all $x$ on the real line and $t \geq 0$), $y(x,0) = f(x)$, and $y_t(x,0) = 0$, where

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \; \phantom{{-1} \leq {} }x < -1, \\ x+1 & \text{if } \; {-1} \leq x < 0, \\ -x+1 & \text{if } \; \phantom{-}0 \leq x < 1, \\ 0 & \text{if } \; \phantom{-}1 < x . \end{cases}$$

Solve using the d'Alembert solution. That is, write down a piecewise definition for the solution. Then sketch the solution for $t=0$, $t={1}/{2}$, $t=1$, and $t=2$.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q: Using the d'Alembert solution solve $y_{tt} = 9y_{xx}$, $0 < x < 1$, $t > 0$, $y(0,t) = y(1, t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = \sin (2 \pi x)$, and $y_t(x,0) = \sin (3 \pi x)$.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
q:
Take $y_{tt} = 4y_{xx}$, $0 < x < 1$, $t > 0$, $y(0,t) = y(1, t) = 0$, $y(x,0) = x-x^2$, and $y_t(x,0) = 0$. Using the d'Alembert solution find the solution at

(a) $t=0.1$,

(b) $t={1}/{2}$,

(c) $t=1$.

You may have to split your answer up by cases.

section_title: D'Alembert solution of the wave equation
Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < \pi$ and $0 < y < \pi$, solve the problem

$$\Delta u = 0, \quad u(x,0) = \sin x, \quad u(x,\pi) = 0, \quad u(0,y) = 0, \quad u(\pi,y) = 0 .$$

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < 1$ and $0 < y < 1$, solve the problem

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, & \\ u(x,0) = \sin (\pi x) - \sin (2\pi x), \quad & u(x,1) = 0, \\ u(0,y) = 0, \quad & u(1,y) = 0 . \end{array}$$

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < 1$ and $0 < y < 1$, solve the problem

$$\begin{aligned}& u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, \\ & u(x,0) = u(x,1) = u(0,y) = u(1,y) = C .\end{aligned}$$

for some constant $C$. Hint: Guess, then check your intuition.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < \pi$ and $0 < y < \pi$, solve

$$\Delta u = 0, \quad u(x,0) = 0, \quad u(x,\pi) = \pi, \quad u(0,y) = y, \quad u(\pi,y) = y .$$

Hint: Try a solution of the form $u(x,y) = X(x) + Y(y)$ (different separation of variables).

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < w$ and $0 < y < h$, solve the problem

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, & \\ u(x,0) = 0, \quad & u(x,h) = f(x), \\ u(0,y) = 0, \quad & u(w,y) = 0. \end{array}$$

The solution should be in series form using the Fourier-series coefficients of $f(x)$.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < w$ and $0 < y < h$, solve the problem

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, & \\ u(x,0) = 0, \quad & u(x,h) = 0, \\ u(0,y) = f(y), \quad & u(w,y) = 0. \end{array}$$

The solution should be in series form using the Fourier-series coefficients of $f(y)$.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < w$ and $0 < y < h$, solve the problem

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, & \\ u(x,0) = 0, \quad & u(x,h) = 0, \\ u(0,y) = 0, \quad & u(w,y) = f(y). \end{array}$$

The solution should be in series form using the Fourier-series coefficients of $f(y)$.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < 1$ and $0 < y < 1$, solve the problem

$$\begin{array}{ll} u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, & \\ u(x,0) = \sin (9 \pi x), \quad & u(x,1) = \sin (2 \pi x), \\ u(0,y) = 0, \quad & u(1,y) = 0 . \end{array}$$

Hint: Use superposition.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < 1$ and $0 < y < 1$, solve the problem

$$\begin{aligned}& u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, \\ & u(x,0) = \sin (\pi x), \quad u(x,1) = \sin (\pi x), \\ & u(0,y) = \sin (\pi y), \quad u(1,y) = \sin (\pi y) .\end{aligned}$$

Hint: Use superposition.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q: Using only your intuition find $u({1}/{2},{1}/{2})$, for the problem $\Delta u = 0$, where $u(0,y) = u(1,y) = 100$ for $0 < y < 1$, and $u(x,0) = u(x,1) = 0$ for $0 < x < 1$. Explain.

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < 1$ and $0 < y < 1$, solve the problem

$$\Delta u = 0, \quad u(x,0) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2} \sin (n \pi x), \quad u(x,1) = 0, \quad u(0,y) = 0, \quad u(1,y) = 0 .$$

section_title: Steady state temperature and the Laplacian
q:
In the region described by $0 < x < 1$ and $0 < y < 2$, solve the problem

$$\Delta u = 0, \quad u(x,0) = 0.1 \sin (\pi x), \quad u(x,2) = 0, \quad u(0,y) = 0, \quad u(1,y) = 0 .$$

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Compute the series for $u(1,\theta)$ and verify that it really is what we have just claimed. Hint: Be careful, make sure not to divide by zero.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Using series, solve $\Delta u = 0$, $u(1,\theta) = \lvert \theta \rvert$, for $-\pi < \theta \leq \pi$.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q:
Using series solve $\Delta u = 0$, $u(1,\theta) = g(\theta)$ for the following data. Hint: trig identities.

(a) $g(\theta) = {1}/{2} + 3\sin(\theta) + \cos(3\theta)$

(b) $g(\theta) = 3\cos(3\theta) + 3\sin(3\theta) + \sin(9\theta)$

(c) $g(\theta) = 2 \cos(\theta+1)$

(d) $g(\theta) = \sin^2(\theta)$

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Using the Poisson kernel, give the solution to $\Delta u = 0$, where $u(1,\theta)$ is zero for $\theta$ outside the interval $[-{\pi}/{4},{\pi}/{4}]$ and $u(1,\theta)$ is 1 for $\theta$ on the interval $[-{\pi}/{4},{\pi}/{4}]$.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q:
(a) Draw a graph for the Poisson kernel as a function of $\alpha$ when $r={1}/{2}$ and $\theta = 0$.

(b) Describe what happens to the graph when you make $r$ bigger (as it approaches 1).

(c) Knowing that the solution $u(r,\theta)$ is the weighted average of $g(\theta)$ with the Poisson kernel as the weight, explain what your answer to part b) means.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Let $g(\theta)$ be the function $xy = \cos \theta \sin \theta$ on the boundary. Use the series solution to find a solution to the Dirichlet problem $\Delta u = 0$, $u(1,\theta) = g(\theta)$. Now convert the solution to Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$. Is this solution surprising? Hint: Use your trig identities.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Carry out the computation we needed in the separation of variables and solve $r^2 R'' + r R' - n^2 R = 0$, for $n=0,1,2,3,\ldots$.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Derive the series solution to the Dirichlet problem if the region is a circle of radius $\rho$ rather than 1. That is, solve $\Delta u = 0$, $u(\rho,\theta) = g(\theta)$.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Using series solve $\Delta u = 0$, $u(1,\theta) = 1+ \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\sin(n\theta)$.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Using the series solution find the solution to $\Delta u = 0$, $u(1,\theta) = 1- \cos(\theta)$. Express the solution in Cartesian coordinates (that is, using $x$ and $y$).

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q:
(a) Try and guess a solution to $\Delta u = -1$, $u(1,\theta) = 0$. Hint: Try a solution that only depends on $r$. Also, don't worry about the boundary condition at first.

(b) Now solve $\Delta u = -1$, $u(1,\theta) = \sin(2\theta)$ using superposition.

section_title: Dirichlet problem in the circle and the Poisson kernel
q: Derive the Poisson kernel solution if the region is a circle of radius $\rho$ rather than 1. That is, solve $\Delta u = 0$, $u(\rho,\theta) = g(\theta)$.

Find eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for

$$y'' + \lambda y = 0, \quad y'(0) = 0, \quad y'(1) = 0.$$

Identify the $p, q, r, \alpha_j, \beta_j$. Can you use the theorem above to make the search for eigenvalues easier? Hint: Consider the condition $-y'(0)=0$.

Find eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of

$$y''+\lambda y = 0, \quad y(0)- y'(0) = 0, \quad y(1) = 0 .$$

Expand the function $f(x) = x$ on $0 \leq x \leq 1$ using eigenfunctions of the system

$$y'' + \lambda y = 0, \quad y'(0) = 0, \quad y(1) = 0 .$$

Suppose that you had a Sturm–Liouville problem on the interval $[0,1]$ and came up with $y_n(x) = \sin (\gamma n x)$, where $\gamma > 0$ is some constant. Decompose $f(x) = x$, $0 < x < 1$ in terms of these eigenfunctions.

Find eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of

$$y^{(4)}+\lambda y = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad y'(0) = 0, \quad y(1) = 0, \quad y'(1) = 0 .$$

This problem is not a Sturm–Liouville problem, but the idea is the same.

Find eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of

$$y'' + \lambda y = 0, \quad y(-1) = 0, \quad y(1) = 0 .$$
Justify $\lambda > 0$ just from the equation for $X$ and the boundary conditions.

Suppose you have a beam of length 5 with free ends. Let $y$ be the transverse deviation of the beam at position $x$ on the beam ($0 < x < 5$). You know that the constants are such that this satisfies the equation $y_{tt} + 4 y_{xxxx} = 0$. Suppose you know that the initial shape of the beam is the graph of $x(5-x)$, and the initial velocity is uniformly equal to 2 (same for each $x$) in the positive $y$ direction. Set up the equation together with the boundary and initial conditions. Just set up, do not solve.

Suppose you have a beam of length 5 with one end free and one end fixed (the fixed end is at $x=5$). Let $u$ be the longitudinal deviation of the beam at position $x$ on the beam ($0 < x < 5$). You know that the constants are such that this satisfies the equation $u_{tt} = 4 u_{xx}$. Suppose you know that the initial displacement of the beam is $\frac{x-5}{50}$, and the initial velocity is $\frac{-(x-5)}{100}$ in the positive $u$ direction. Set up the equation together with the boundary and initial conditions. Just set up, do not solve.

Suppose you have

$$\begin{aligned} & a^4 y_{xxxx} + y_{tt} = 0 \quad (0 < x < 1, t > 0) , \\ & y(0,t) = y_{xx}(0,t) = 0,\\ & y(1,t) = y_{xx}(1,t) = 0 ,\\ & y(x,0) = f(x), \quad y_{t}(x,0) = g(x) . \end{aligned}$$

That is, you also have an initial velocity. Find a series solution. Hint: Use the same idea as we did for the wave equation.

Suppose you have a beam of length 1 with hinged ends. Let $y$ be the transverse deviation of the beam at position $x$ on the beam ($0 < x < 1$). You know that the constants are such that this satisfies the equation $y_{tt} + 4 y_{xxxx} = 0$. Suppose you know that the initial shape of the beam is the graph of $\sin (\pi x)$, and the initial velocity is 0. Solve for $y$.

Suppose you have a beam of length 10 with two fixed ends. Let $y$ be the transverse deviation of the beam at position $x$ on the beam ($0 < x < 10$). You know that the constants are such that this satisfies the equation $y_{tt} + 9 y_{xxxx} = 0$. Suppose you know that the initial shape of the beam is the graph of $\sin^2(\pi x)$, and the initial velocity is equal to $x(10-x)$. Set up the equation together with the boundary and initial conditions. Just set up, do not solve.
Check that $y_p$ works.
Suppose that the forcing function for the vibrating string is $F_0 \sin (\omega t)$. Derive the particular solution $y_p$.

The units are cgs (centimeters-grams-seconds). For $k=0.005$, $\omega = 1.991 \times {10}^{-7}$, $A_0 = 20$. Find the depth at which the temperature variation is half ($\pm 10$ degrees) of what it is on the surface.
Derive the solution for underground temperature oscillation without assuming that $T_0 = 0$.

Take the forced vibrating string. Suppose that $L=1$, $a=1$. Suppose that the forcing function is a triangle wave, $\lvert t \rvert -\frac{\pi}{2}$ on $-\pi < t < \pi$ extended periodically. Find the particular solution.
The units are cgs (centimeters-grams-seconds). For $k=0.01$, $\omega = 1.991 \times {10}^{-7}$, $A_0 = 25$. Find the depth at which the summer is again the hottest point.
Verify the theorem. That is, show that $\mathcal{L} \bigl\{ A f(t) + B g(t) \bigr\} = A \mathcal{L} \bigl\{ f(t) \bigr\} + B \mathcal{L} \bigl\{ g(t) \bigr\}$.

Use L'Hopital's rule from calculus to show that a polynomial is of exponential order. Hint: Note that a sum of two exponential-order functions is also of exponential order. Then show that $t^n$ is of exponential order for any $n$.
Derive the first shifting property from the definition of the Laplace transform.
Find the Laplace transform of $3+t^5+\sin (\pi t)$.
Find the Laplace transform of $a+bt+ct^2$ for some constants $a$, $b$, and $c$.
Find the Laplace transform of $A \cos (\omega t) + B \sin (\omega t)$.
Find the Laplace transform of $\cos^2 (\omega t)$.
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $\frac{4}{s^2-9}$.
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $\frac{2s}{s^2-1}$.
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $\frac{1}{{(s-1)}^2(s+1)}$.
Find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = \begin{cases} t & \text{if } \; t \geq 1, \\ 0 & \text{if } \; t < 1. \end{cases}$
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $\frac{s}{(s^2+s+2)(s+4)}$.
Find the Laplace transform of $\sin\bigl(\omega (t-a)\bigr)$.
Find the Laplace transform of $t\sin(\omega t)$. Hint: Several integrations by parts.
Find the Laplace transform of $4{(t+1)}^2$.
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $\frac{8}{s^3(s+2)}$.
Find the Laplace transform of $te^{-t}$. Hint: Shifting property.
Find the Laplace transform of $\sin(t)e^{-t}$. Hint: Integrate by parts.
Using the Heaviside function write down the piecewise function that is 0 for $t < 0$, $t^2$ for $t$ in $[0,1]$ and $t$ for $t > 1$.

Using the Laplace transform solve

$$m x'' + c x' + k x = 0 , \quad x(0) = a, \quad x'(0) = b ,$$

where $m > 0$, $c > 0$, $k > 0$, and $c^2 - 4km > 0$ (system is overdamped).

Using the Laplace transform solve

$$m x'' + c x' + k x = 0 , \quad x(0) = a, \quad x'(0) = b ,$$

where $m > 0$, $c > 0$, $k > 0$, and $c^2 - 4km < 0$ (system is underdamped).

Using the Laplace transform solve

$$m x'' + c x' + k x = 0 , \quad x(0) = a, \quad x'(0) = b ,$$

where $m > 0$, $c > 0$, $k > 0$, and $c^2 = 4km$ (system is critically damped).
Solve $x'' + x = u(t-1)$ for initial conditions $x(0) = 0$ and $x'(0) = 0$.

Show the “differentiation of the transform” property. Suppose $\mathcal{L} \bigl\{ f(t) \bigr\} = F(s)$, then show

$$\mathcal{L} \bigl\{ -t f(t) \bigr\} = F'(s) .$$

Hint: Differentiate under the integral sign.
Solve $x''' + x = t^3 u(t-1)$ for initial conditions $x(0) = 1$ and $x'(0) = 0$, $x''(0) = 0$.
Using the definition of the Laplace transform, justify the second shifting property: $\mathcal{L} \bigl\{ f(t-a) \, u(t-a) \bigr\} = e^{-as} \mathcal{L} \bigl\{ f(t) \bigr\}$.

Define

$$f(t) = \begin{cases} {(t-1)}^2 & \text{if } \; 1 \leq t < 2, \\ 3-t & \text{if } \; 2 \leq t < 3, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} . \end{cases}$$

(a) Sketch the graph of $f(t)$.

(b) Write down $f(t)$ using the Heaviside function.

(c) Solve $x''+x=f(t)$, $x(0)=0$, $x'(0) = 0$ using the Laplace transform.
Find the transfer function for $m x'' + c x' + kx = f(t)$, $x(0)=0$, $x'(0)=0$.

Suppose $Lx = f(t)$, $x(0)=0$, $x'(0)=0$ for the input function $f(t) = t$ gives the output $x(t) = 2e^{-t} + te^{-t} + (t-2)$.

(a) Find $F(s)$, $X(s)$, and the transfer function $H(s)$.

(b) If the input is instead $f(t) = \sin(t)$, find the new output $x(t)$.
Suppose $f(t) = 1$ if $0 \leq t < 1$ and $f(t)=0$ if $1 \leq t < 2$, and then extend periodically for all $t \geq 0$ so that $f(t)=f(t+2)$. Compute the Laplace transform $F(s)$.

Using the Heaviside function $u(t)$, write down the function

$$f(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \; \phantom{1 \leq {}} t < 1 , \\ t-1 & \text{if } \; 1 \leq t < 2 , \\ 1 & \text{if } \; 2 \leq t . \end{cases}$$
